Separately, the malaria vaccines RTS, S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M were recom- mended by WHO in October 2021 and October 2023, respectively.11 Therapeutic or curative antibody therapy (passive immuno- therapy) is given after infection or after symptom onset to treat established infection. Antibody therapies may be used for either prevention or treatment, and both applications involve distinct clinical goals. Examples include monoclonal antibody therapy for Ebola and the use of rabies immunoglobulin for rabies.12,13 For malaria, monoclonal antibodies such as CIS43LS are under clin- ical investigation primarily as prophylactic interventions rather than as treatments for established infection.14 While single-cell transcriptomics is a discovery tool, when used in infectious disease research, it may help identify stage-specific expression states and candidate antigens that could inform antibody studies, while structural analyses can characterize determinants of antibody binding and genomic analyses can identify potential escape variants emerging during persistent infection (Fig. 1).15,16 Related genomic approaches have also been used to investigate viral variants associated with antibody escape in infectious diseases such as COVID-19. Transcriptomic maps may guide the discovery of future small- molecule targets. For instance, M5717, a Plasmodium eukaryotic translation elongation factor 2 inhibitor evaluated as a small- molecule antimalarial, has shown preclinical evidence of parasite clearance when combined with pyronaridine.17 Its identification is not attributed to single-cell transcriptomics. This distinction clari- fies that single-cell transcriptomics may help prioritize translation- related vulnerabilities, while other approaches are required to develop and deliver corresponding interventions. Mutations in pathogen proteins can confer antibody resistance when they result in reduced susceptibility to the parental antibody. Selecting for such mutants resistant to the particular parent antibody in cell culture is an established approach for studying antibody resistance,18 while antibody-driven escape variants have also been observed during persistent infection.16 Therefore, designing antibodies to target such proteins could, in principle, support the development of more escape-resistant thera- peutic antibodies. The central concept proposed here is that anti- body strategies might be combined with single-cell transcrip- tomics mapping of candidate proteins and variants to reduce the potential for parasite escape. This could represent a future thera- peutic strategy, but it requires experimental and clinical validation. Conventional drug pipelines have not failed; they have adapted and continue to deliver. Artemisinin combination therapy and emerging combinations such as ganaplacide-lumefantrine remain essential. Single-cell transcriptomics complements rather than replaces these approaches by adding resolution to parasite tran- scriptional plasticity that may be associated with tolerance and transmission. Future antibodies tailored to validated parasite anti- gens could potentially contribute to parasite inhibition, pending further validation.19 Barriers that block translation to human health include cost and access. Protection from some monoclonal antibodies can last for months,14 However, dosing, delivery, data integration challenges, the complexity of translating transcriptomic signatures into clinic- ally actionable therapeutic targets, and affordability may limit their use in low-income countries where the burden is highest.20 Single-cell transcriptomic analyses may also be affected by sampling and cell-recovery biases, which can influence the apparent representation of parasite stages and transcriptional states. Key proteins highlighted by single-cell transcriptomic studies require independent experimental, pharmacological, and clinical validation before they can be considered druggable targets. Addressing these challenges will require human-focused optimiza- tion, such as the application of optimized dose regimens, delivery Ozurumba-Dwight L.N.: Transcriptomics and Ab therapy dual strategy Gene Expr DOI: 10.14218/GE.2026.00028 | Volume 25 Issue 4, October 2026 3 routes, and formulations informed by human pharmacokinetics. Single-cell transcriptomics is a discovery and profiling method, not itself a treatment. Its power lies in decoding stage-specific transcription and cellular heterogeneity in Plasmodium parasites and identifying relevant states and candidates. Nanobodies could be considered “precision antibodies” when their targets are selected using identified variant information from single-cell transcriptomics. Transcriptomics could be used to identify antigens highly expressed during vulnerable stages or in drug-resistant subpopulations. Generally, future antibodies could be bioengineered using target-selection strategies informed by large single-cell transcriptomic datasets, together with predictive tools such as machine learning and artificial intelligence to identify antigens or molecular targets with a high likelihood of developing resistance-associated alterations. Such approaches could better guide the selection and use of appropriate neutralizing antibodies before resistance emerges (Fig. 1). Single-cell transcriptomics decodes stage-specific gene expression, transcriptional heterogeneity, and parasite adaptation. Antibody immunotherapy informed by such transcriptomic maps could support more precise interventions. Genetic mutations (such as PfK13, PfCRT, PfMDR1, PfDHFR, and PfDHPS) remain central to resistance, while transcriptional adaptation may provide additional layers of regulation that single-cell transcriptomics may help illuminate. Single-cell transcriptomics may help identify parasite-stage vulnerabilities and guide future target discovery, while antibody-based prevention and other precision interventions require further validation for affordability, delivery, durability, and clinical impact. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the challenge of antimalarial drug resistance, which remains a major obstacle in malaria control efforts, and explores the potential of single-cell transcriptomics and antibody immunotherapy as a dual strategy to combat this issue.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study presents a conceptual framework combining single-cell RNA sequencing with antibody immunotherapy, focusing on Plasmodium falciparum and related species, and outlines the potential for this approach to identify and target drug-resistant parasite subpopulations.
analysis.methods: The methods involve using single-cell RNA sequencing to map transcriptional heterogeneity and identify stage-specific vulnerabilities, combined with antibody immunotherapy informed by these transcriptomic insights, and leveraging machine learning and artificial intelligence to guide target selection.
analysis.main_results: The study reports decreased susceptibility to dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors in Ugandan Plasmodium falciparum isolates and highlights epigenetically conferred ring-stage survival against artemisinin treatment.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that single-cell transcriptomics can help identify parasite-stage vulnerabilities and guide future target discovery, while antibody-based prevention and other precision interventions require further validation for affordability, delivery, durability, and clinical impact.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that integrating single-cell transcriptomics with antibody immunotherapy could help mitigate the emergence of drug-resistant clones and reduce recrudescence and transmission-specific stages of malaria.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study acknowledges limitations such as sampling and cell-recovery biases, as well as challenges in translating transcriptomic signatures into clinically actionable targets, and notes that the evidence is moderate due to the conceptual nature of the framework.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the potential of combining single-cell transcriptomics with antibody immunotherapy as a dual strategy to combat antimalarial drug resistance. It highlights the challenges posed by genetic and epigenetic adaptations in Plasmodium falciparum and related species, emphasizing the need for identifying and targeting drug-resistant parasite subpopulations. The proposed approach aims to suppress resistant clones and address mechanisms of escape associated with drug-resistance genes, particularly if validated targets are associated with these subpopulations. The study outlines the use of single-cell RNA sequencing to map transcriptional heterogeneity and identify stage-specific vulnerabilities, which can inform the development of antibody-based interventions. However, it acknowledges limitations such as sampling biases and challenges in translating transcriptomic data into clinical applications. The findings suggest that this strategy could complement existing approaches targeting metabolic resistance pathways and may help reduce recrudescence and transmission-specific stages of malaria. The evidence is moderate due to the conceptual nature of the framework and the need for further validation.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究解决了抗疟药物耐药性的挑战,这仍然是疟疾控制工作的一个主要障碍,并探讨了单细胞转录组学和抗体免疫疗法作为解决这一问题的双重策略的潜力。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究提出了一个将单细胞 RNA 测序与抗体免疫疗法相结合的概念框架,重点关注恶性疟原虫和相关物种,并概述了这种方法识别和靶向耐药寄生虫亚群的潜力。
elements_zh.methods: 这些方法包括使用单细胞 RNA 测序来绘制转录异质性并识别特定阶段的漏洞,结合这些转录组学见解提供的抗体免疫疗法,并利用机器学习和人工智能来指导靶点选择。
elements_zh.main_results: 该研究报告乌干达恶性疟原虫分离株对二氢叶酸还原酶抑制剂的敏感性降低,并强调表观遗传学赋予青蒿素 治疗 的环期存活率。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,单细胞转录组学可以帮助识别寄生虫阶段的漏洞并指导未来的目标发现,而基于抗体的预防和其他精准干预措施需要进一步验证可负担性、交付、耐久性和临床影响。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,将单细胞转录组学与抗体免疫疗法相结合有助于减少耐药克隆的出现,并减少疟疾的复发和 传播 特定阶段。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究承认采样和细胞回收偏差等局限性,以及将转录组特征转化为临床可操作目标的挑战,并指出由于该框架的概念性质,证据是温和的。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the challenge of antimalarial drug resistance, which remains a major obstacle in malaria control efforts, and explores the potential of single-cell transcriptomics and antibody immunotherapy as a dual strategy to combat this issue.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study presents a conceptual framework combining single-cell RNA sequencing with antibody immunotherapy, focusing on Plasmodium falciparum and related species, and outlines the potential for this approach to identify and target drug-resistant parasite subpopulations.
analysis_en.methods: The methods involve using single-cell RNA sequencing to map transcriptional heterogeneity and identify stage-specific vulnerabilities, combined with antibody immunotherapy informed by these transcriptomic insights, and leveraging machine learning and artificial intelligence to guide target selection.
analysis_en.main_results: The study reports decreased susceptibility to dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors in Ugandan Plasmodium falciparum isolates and highlights epigenetically conferred ring-stage survival against artemisinin treatment.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that single-cell transcriptomics can help identify parasite-stage vulnerabilities and guide future target discovery, while antibody-based prevention and other precision interventions require further validation for affordability, delivery, durability, and clinical impact.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that integrating single-cell transcriptomics with antibody immunotherapy could help mitigate the emergence of drug-resistant clones and reduce recrudescence and transmission-specific stages of malaria.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study acknowledges limitations such as sampling and cell-recovery biases, as well as challenges in translating transcriptomic signatures into clinically actionable targets, and notes that the evidence is moderate due to the conceptual nature of the framework.
